AWS AMPLIFY: AN INTRODUCTION AND WHY IT FITS STUDENT AND PERSONAL PROJECTS Many of us have finished a frontend in no time, only to spend days on the backend, database setup, login features and deployment. AWS Amplify is designed to reduce that overhead so you can focus on the logic of your application instead of the infrastructure beneath it.
Key points to know:
Authentication: Amplify integrates Amazon Cognito with a few CLI commands or simple configuration steps. Sign-up, sign-in, password reset and session management are available out of the box. API and database: You can create a GraphQL API with AWS AppSync or a REST API with API Gateway and DynamoDB, so reading and writing data from the frontend stays simple. Hosting and CI/CD: Amplify connects directly to GitHub or GitLab. Each git push triggers an automatic build and deployment. Serverless architecture: There are no servers to maintain, and costs stay low for small projects. Framework support: Amplify works well with React, Next.js, Vue, Flutter and React Native. Best fit: Demos, course projects and MVPs (minimum viable products). Limitation: Deep infrastructure customization, such as a dedicated VPC or complex IAM permissions, takes extra study, because Amplify creates many of these resources automatically and you need to understand them before changing them. AWS Amplify helps you follow a professional cloud workflow while saving time, especially for beginners who want to ship a working product.

Summary Report: “ The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” Event Objectives The event aimed to provide participants with a practical perspective on AI Agents and AI-powered applications. Instead of focusing only on AI technology itself, the talkshow introduced the way developers think about real-world problems when building AI-powered bots.
The event also provided an opportunity to learn from experienced developers and technical leaders, understand how AI is being applied in enterprise environments, and gain insights into career opportunities in the technology industry.
Speakers Thien Lu – Program Manager, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Truong Bui – Tech Lead, CMC Global Phong Pham – Program Manager, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Key Highlights Understanding AI Agents One of the main topics of the event was AI Agents and how they can be used to build applications that are more capable of handling real-world tasks.
The discussion helped me understand that building an AI-powered bot is not simply about connecting an application to an AI model. Developers also need to think about the problem that the bot is solving, how users interact with it, and how the system should process information and respond.
Real-World Programming Problems The event connected AI concepts with practical programming situations. This showed how developers need to consider actual user and business requirements instead of focusing only on the technical capabilities of AI.
I learned that a good AI solution should begin with a clearly defined problem and then determine how AI can provide value to the users.
The Thinking Behind Building a Bot The most interesting part of the event was understanding the thought process behind building an AI bot.
Rather than immediately selecting technologies, developers should first consider:
What problem does the bot need to solve? Who will use the bot? What information does the bot need? What should the bot be able to do? How should the bot respond to different situations? How can the system be designed to work reliably in a real environment? This changed my perspective from simply “using AI” to designing a complete AI solution around a specific problem.
Enterprise Perspective The event also provided a perspective from CMC Global about how AI can be applied in a professional environment.
This helped me understand that enterprise AI applications need to consider not only functionality but also practical requirements such as reliability, security, scalability, and the actual business value provided by the system.
Career and Industry Insights At the end of the event, participants also had opportunities to interact with representatives from CMC Global regarding career opportunities, interviews, and professional development.
This gave me a better understanding of the skills that developers should develop when preparing to work in an AI-related software engineering environment.
Key Takeaways Technical Perspective
AI Agents can be used to create applications that perform more complex tasks than traditional chatbot systems. Building an AI application requires more than selecting an AI model. The AI component needs to be integrated into a complete application and workflow. Real-world AI systems should consider reliability, security, scalability, and user requirements. Problem-Solving Mindset
The biggest lesson I gained from the event was to start with the problem rather than the technology.
Before choosing AWS services or AI models, developers should understand the business requirements and define what the system actually needs to accomplish.
Breaking a complex problem into smaller components also makes it easier to design and implement the solution.
Career Perspective The event also showed me that AI development requires a combination of different skills. Understanding AI is important, but software development fundamentals, problem-solving, system design, and the ability to understand business requirements are also necessary.
Applying to My FCAJ Project The knowledge from this event can be directly applied to my FCAJ project, which focuses on building an AI assistant for enterprise legal and security information.
Before attending the event, I mainly focused on identifying which AWS services could be used, such as Amazon Bedrock, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB.
After the event, I realized that the more important first step is to clearly define the problem that the system needs to solve.
For example, an enterprise user could describe a security or legal incident to the AI assistant. The system would then use the organization’s internal knowledge base to analyze the situation and provide relevant information.
This approach helps me think about the project from the business use case first, and then determine how AWS services and AI technologies should be used to implement the solution.
Event Experience Learning from Experienced Speakers The event allowed me to learn from technical leaders and program managers who have experience working with technology and AI projects. Their perspectives helped me better understand how AI solutions are approached in real-world environments.
Understanding Real-World AI Development Instead of learning AI only from theoretical materials, the event showed how developers need to think about practical problems when creating AI-powered applications.
This helped me connect the AI concepts I am studying with actual software development.
Problem-Solving and Technical Thinking The event encouraged me to think more carefully about the reasoning behind an AI solution. I learned that choosing a technology should come after understanding the problem and requirements.
This is particularly useful for my FCAJ project because AWS provides many different services, and choosing a service should be based on the actual requirements rather than simply using as many services as possible.
Career Discussion The career discussion with CMC Global also gave me an opportunity to learn more about the expectations of companies in the technology industry.
It encouraged me to improve not only my technical knowledge but also my ability to explain projects, solve problems, and work effectively as part of a team.
Lessons Learned The most important lesson I gained from the event is that building an AI solution is not simply about using a powerful AI model.
A useful AI application requires a clear problem, a suitable workflow, appropriate data, good system design, and consideration of real-world requirements.
This mindset will help me approach my FCAJ project more systematically and make better decisions when selecting AWS services and designing the AI workflow.

title: Introduction
content:
Concepts RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieve the relevant passages first (Retrieval), add them to the prompt (Augmentation), and then have the model answer based only on those passages (Generation). Knowledge base on DynamoDB: legal provisions are stored as items in a DynamoDB table and searched by keyword. This approach is simple and fits within the AWS Free Tier, but it does not understand meaning the way vector search does. Serverless: Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB scale automatically and charge based on usage, which suits low-budget projects. Groq API: an external inference service that runs the language model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b), called by Lambda over HTTPS. Problem and goal Staff need quick answers about personal data regulations, for example whether they can use a customer’s citizen ID (CCCD) data for marketing. Public chatbots may invent legal provisions or cite them incorrectly. The goal is for answers to rely only on the legal texts the team provides, running on AWS at near-zero cost.
Architecture and data flow Data flow:
The user opens the website on S3, types a question into the chat window, and sends it. index.html sends an HTTP POST over HTTPS to API Gateway. API Gateway checks CORS and passes the payload to the Lambda function. Lambda queries the LegalArticles DynamoDB table for provisions related to the question (function retrieve_legal_context). DynamoDB returns the matching provisions to Lambda as legal context. Lambda builds the complete prompt (system prompt, legal context, and question) and calls the Groq API. Groq returns the answer as text to Lambda. Lambda formats a standard JSON response, including an error code if applicable, and returns it to API Gateway. API Gateway returns the result, and the chat window displays it. Lambda logs are written to Amazon CloudWatch throughout the process. Components Component AWS service / resource Prompt and RAG logic Lambda (Python) Knowledge base DynamoDB, LegalArticles table Backend API API Gateway + Lambda Frontend S3 static website, index.html Security and operations CloudWatch, Budgets, IAM Implemented vs. planned The implemented system differs from the original design in several areas. The table below shows what is currently in place.
Item Original design Current implementation Knowledge base S3 + Bedrock Knowledge Bases DynamoDB LegalArticles table (keyword lookup) LLM Amazon Bedrock Groq API (outside AWS) Frontend AWS Amplify S3 static website Authentication Cognito Not yet (public API) Response format Structured: risk level, provisions, evidence Text answer wrapped in JSON Conversation history DynamoDB Not yet implemented Incident reporting and alerts SNS Not yet implemented AI safety principles This is a preliminary assessment, not an official legal conclusion. Answers rely only on the provided legal provisions. The system must not invent provisions or citations. If the database has no supporting basis, the system must say so.

title: Blog 2
content:
AWS LEARNING CORNER: WHAT NEWCOMERS NEED TO KNOW TO AVOID A SHOCKING END-OF-MONTH BILL One common situation for people new to AWS is turning on a test resource, forgetting to turn it off, and then receiving an unexpected bill at the end of the month. Cost control is not only about peace of mind while you practice. It is also a fundamental skill in cloud infrastructure management.
Below are the key settings and tips for managing your budget effectively from the very beginning.
1. Set up AWS Budgets and Billing Alerts This is the first step you should take right after creating your AWS account.
How it works: Set a safe budget threshold (for example, $5 or $10). When actual or forecast costs exceed this threshold, the system automatically sends you an email notification. Benefit: Resources running in the background for long periods are caught early. 2. Use the AWS Free Tier wisely The Free Tier includes many free resources, but each comes with specific conditions:
Time limits: For example, EC2 offers 750 hours per month for t2.micro or t3.micro instances (depending on the Region). If you run two instances continuously, usage is counted twice and you can quickly exceed the free allowance. Capacity limits: S3 and EBS have specific rules on storage capacity and number of requests. Read the service terms carefully before you create resources. 3. Clean up unused resources Idle or standalone resources are often the source of hidden costs:
Stop or terminate EC2 instances: Shut down test servers when you are not working on them. Note on Elastic IPs: An Elastic IP is free only when it is attached to a running EC2 instance. If you detach it, or attach it to a stopped instance, you will still be charged for keeping it allocated. Unattached EBS volumes and snapshots: When you delete an EC2 instance, some EBS volumes or automatically created snapshots may remain and keep incurring storage charges. 4. Monitor details with AWS Cost Explorer Visual tool: AWS Cost Explorer provides charts that break down costs over time, by service, or by tag. Regular checks: Reviewing cost reports once or twice a week helps you quickly spot services that are consuming your budget unexpectedly. Conclusion Cost optimization and control are an essential part of thinking like a cloud professional. Setting up a safe environment from the start lets you learn and experiment with AWS services without worrying about the bill.

title: Proposal
content:
Legal RAG Platform: Automated Legal Advisory System for Decree 13/2023/ND-CP A Unified AWS Serverless Solution with LLM for Real-Time Legal Research and Analysis 1. Executive Summary The Legal RAG Platform is an automated advisory system that helps users and team members quickly look up and analyze complex Vietnamese legal regulations. It focuses on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP on personal data protection. The platform is built on a fully serverless architecture on AWS and uses a large language model (LLM) from the Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b). Answers are grounded in the actual legal text, which reduces the risk of AI hallucination. The platform also keeps operating costs at $0 by staying within the AWS Free Tier.
2. Problem Statement The Problem Legal documents such as Decree 13/2023/ND-CP are long, dense, and difficult for non-experts to search manually. General-purpose AI tools, such as the free version of ChatGPT, often lack in-depth knowledge of Vietnamese law. They tend to give generic answers without an accurate legal basis. Building a self-hosted AI system is expensive in hardware and complex to operate. The Solution The platform uses an automated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline. When a user submits a question, the system searches the database for the most relevant legal provisions and injects them into a System Prompt. The LLM then generates an answer that cites those provisions clearly.
Amazon DynamoDB stores the extracted legal provisions in the LegalArticles table. AWS Lambda handles the backend logic, and Amazon API Gateway exposes a stable API endpoint. Groq API with the qwen/qwen3.8-27b model generates clear, coherent answers. Amazon S3 Static Website hosts the web interface, where users interact through a chat window. Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI) High accuracy: Answers stay close to the provided legal text and are transparent and well-supported. Cost efficiency: The serverless design runs within the AWS Free Tier, with monthly costs close to $0. Scalability: The decoupled architecture makes it easy to add new legal documents, such as the Law on Network Information Security or the Law on Information Technology, to DynamoDB in the future. 3. Solution Architecture The system follows a serverless architecture that connects the frontend, backend, and external LLM in a closed loop.
AWS Services and Technologies Amazon S3 Static Website: Hosts and serves the static web interface (index.html, CSS, and JavaScript). Amazon API Gateway: Provides a public HTTP/REST API, handles CORS, and forwards client requests to Lambda. AWS Lambda (Python): Runs the RAG logic, queries DynamoDB, and calls the Groq API. Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles): Stores legal provisions and supports fast keyword-based lookup. Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b): Generates and analyzes natural language based on the legal context provided. Component Design Frontend: Users open the website hosted on S3 and enter a question in the chat window. The browser sends an HTTP POST request containing the question over HTTPS to API Gateway. API Gateway: Receives the request, validates CORS settings, and forwards the payload to the Lambda function. Data Retrieval (DynamoDB): The retrieve_legal_context function searches the LegalArticles table for relevant provisions. For example, it can retrieve rules on handling violations involving citizen identity numbers (CCCD) and personal data under Decree 13. Augmentation and Generation (Groq API): Lambda combines the user’s question with the retrieved legal context into a System Prompt with strict constraints, which require answers to be based only on the provided context. It then calls the Groq API. Response Flow: Groq returns the result to Lambda. Lambda formats a standard JSON response and sends it back through API Gateway to display in the chat window. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases Phase 1, Prompt Design and RAG Mechanism: Write a System Prompt that defines the role of a legal expert and sets a context constraint that prohibits fabricated information. Phase 2, Backend and Database: Create the DynamoDB LegalArticles table. Write the Python code for AWS Lambda, including the retrieval function and the Groq API integration. Configure API Gateway, enable CORS headers, and implement standardized error handling. This covers codes 400 and 502/504, as well as code 429 when the Groq API rate limit is exceeded. Phase 3, Testing and Refinement: Send HTTP POST requests with curl and test directly in the web interface. Monitor logs in Amazon CloudWatch. 5. Timeline & Milestones Research and Design: Define the legal scope (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP) and design the RAG data flow. Development and Deployment: Build the DynamoDB database, complete the Lambda function, and configure API Gateway. Integration and Testing: Connect the S3 static website to API Gateway, test the accuracy of answers from the Groq LLM, and refine error handling. 6. Budget Estimation AWS Infrastructure Amazon S3: Free within Free Tier limits. Amazon API Gateway: Free for the first 1 million requests per month. AWS Lambda: Free for up to 1 million requests per month. Amazon DynamoDB: Free within 25 GB of storage and 25 WCU and 25 RCU. Total AWS cost: $0.00 per month.
Groq API The project uses the free tier for the open-source model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b).
Total project investment: VND 0 ($0).
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix API overload (Groq API rate limit, error 429): Implement error handling and display a clear, user-friendly message in the chat interface when the request limit is temporarily exceeded. Inaccurate AI answers (hallucination): Strengthen the System Prompt so the model uses only the legal context retrieved from DynamoDB and does not infer beyond that source. CORS errors in the browser: Configure full CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, POST, OPTIONS) directly in API Gateway. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Achievements A complete serverless backend that scales automatically, runs reliably, and operates at $0 cost.
Practical Value A standardized API gateway and an intuitive chat interface that enable fast, accurate lookup of the core provisions of Decree 13/2023/ND-CP. The platform supports both study and research.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS LEARNING CORNER: BUILDING A SIMPLE, SECURE STATIC WEBSITE WITH S3 + CLOUDFRONT + ROUTE 53 Once you have finished a static website (plain HTML/CSS/JS, or a build from React, Vue or Next.js), the next question is how to host it and deliver it to the internet. The usual goals are low cost, fast access, secure HTTPS and no server to manage.
The combination of Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront and Amazon Route 53 is a standard architecture that addresses these goals well.
Step 1: Store files with Amazon S3 Create an S3 bucket to hold all the built files of your website. Configure the S3 bucket policy and grant access appropriately. Enable Static website hosting and set the default files, for example index.html and 404.html. Step 2: Speed up and secure delivery with Amazon CloudFront (CDN) Create a CloudFront distribution and set the S3 bucket as its origin. Faster delivery: Website content is cached at edge locations around the world, which reduces latency for users. Security: Use a free SSL/TLS certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to enable HTTPS. Also configure Origin Access Control (OAC) to block direct access to the S3 bucket, so traffic can only come through CloudFront. Step 3: Route your domain with Amazon Route 53 Create a hosted zone for your domain in Route 53. Create an A record (alias type) that points your root domain or subdomain to the CloudFront distribution. Technical value and lessons learned Cost optimization: A serverless architecture has no server maintenance costs (Nginx or Apache). For low traffic or personal projects, the monthly cost is close to zero. Scalability: CloudFront’s CDN network absorbs sudden traffic spikes automatically, without infrastructure upgrades. Simpler operations: There is no need to patch operating systems or renew SSL certificates manually. Conclusion This classic hands-on exercise is important because it teaches you how to combine basic AWS services into a complete, secure, industry-standard system.

Steps
Write a role definition (an expert in Vietnamese personal data law). Require the answer to be written in Vietnamese and to cite the legal provisions used. Add a disclaimer: the answer is preliminary and not official legal advice. Check: the model responds with the intended role and tone.
5.3.2 Set context constraints Goal: Force the model to answer only from legal texts retrieved from the database.
Steps
Add a strict rule: answer only from the provided legal texts, and do not fabricate or infer beyond that source. Add a fallback: if the provided text is insufficient, state clearly that there is not enough basis. Test with an out-of-scope question, such as a tax question. Check: an out-of-scope question returns “insufficient basis” instead of a fabricated answer.
5.3.3 Define the input data structure Goal: Decide how Lambda injects DynamoDB data into the outgoing prompt.
Steps
Format each retrieved provision as a labeled block (article number and content). Place the legal context before the user’s question in the message. Limit the number and length of provisions so the prompt stays within the model’s rate and token limits. Check: the printed prompt contains all three parts in the correct order.

content:
Summary Report: “AWS Cloud Architecture, Software Factories, and Career Growth” Event Objectives The event aimed to provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of modern cloud architecture, focusing on serverless computing and asynchronous systems. Instead of just covering theoretical concepts, the sessions introduced real-world lessons from building software factories at scale. The event also provided an opportunity to learn from experienced professionals about preparing for a career in the cloud industry, bridging the gap between universities and businesses, and navigating technical internships and open-source contributions.
Speakers Thinh Nguyen - SYL Solution Henry Duc Bui - CloudThinker Hung Tran - NAB Dao Luong - FCAJ Khang Duong - FCAJ Tuan Tran - FCAJ Key Highlights Building Software Factories at Scale The event started with practical lessons on building “software factories.” The discussion helped me understand the common pitfalls teams face when scaling software development. It highlighted that building at scale requires not just good code, but standardized processes, automation, and practical insights from teams who have successfully done it in enterprise environments.
Bridging the Education and Industry Gap The education session provided a valuable perspective on what students need to prepare before entering the cloud industry. It emphasized that academic knowledge must be paired with hands-on technical skills to bridge the gap between university expectations and actual business requirements.
Rethinking Serverless with AWS Lambda One of the most technical and interesting parts of the event was the deep dive into AWS Lambda Web Functions. The session explained how native HTTP support and 128-request multi-concurrency are redefining Serverless compute. It showed how eliminating adapter overhead and leveraging Active CPU Billing can maximize cost efficiency, providing compelling live performance benchmarks comparing Serverless with Docker on EC2/ECS.
Building Asynchronous Systems with Amazon SQS The event connected architectural concepts with practical system design by exploring Amazon SQS. I learned why modern systems heavily rely on asynchronous processing to decouple services and scale effectively. The session provided concrete design patterns and practical tips for implementing SQS in real-world applications.
Career Growth: Internships and Open Source The latter half of the event focused on career development. Hearing about a real 3-month AWS internship journey—specifically how AWS services were applied to actual projects—provided actionable advice. Furthermore, the session on open-source contributing broke down how to make a first contribution from scratch, build a steady habit, and leverage this to accelerate skill and career growth.
Key Takeaways Technical Perspective
Serverless architecture is evolving rapidly. Features like multi-concurrency and Active CPU Billing in AWS Lambda drastically improve performance and cost-efficiency. Modern, scalable cloud applications require decoupled architectures, making tools like Amazon SQS essential for handling asynchronous workflows smoothly. Building scalable software requires standardized practices (“software factories”) rather than just writing standalone code. System Design Mindset The biggest lesson I gained from the architectural sessions was the importance of choosing the right compute and messaging models. Before deploying an API or a processing job, developers must consider if the task should be synchronous (using optimized Lambda functions) or asynchronous (decoupled via SQS queues) to prevent bottlenecks and ensure system reliability.
Career Perspective The event showed me that entering the cloud industry requires proactive preparation. Technical skills are crucial, but real-world experience—gained through internships, applying AWS to practical projects, and consistently contributing to open-source communities—is what truly differentiates a candidate.
Applying to My FCAJ Project The knowledge from this event can be directly and immediately applied to my FCAJ project, where I am building an AWS Serverless Legal RAG Assistant.
Before this event, I had already set up the core infrastructure using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, API Gateway, DynamoDB, and a React frontend hosted on S3. However, the sessions on AWS Lambda and Amazon SQS gave me new ideas for optimizing my architecture:
Applying AWS Lambda Optimizations: My legal-ai-chat-lambda currently handles requests from API Gateway. Learning about Lambda’s multi-concurrency and Active CPU Billing helps me understand how to optimize my function’s execution time and manage costs more effectively when multiple users query the legal assistant simultaneously. Applying Amazon SQS for Document Processing: Currently, legal documents are stored in my fcaj-raw-docs S3 bucket before being processed into chunks. The SQS session inspired me to decouple this data pipeline. I can implement an Amazon SQS queue between S3 and the processing service to handle document ingestion asynchronously. This ensures that if the system receives a massive batch of legal documents, the architecture can scale gracefully without throttling or crashing. This event helped me shift my mindset from just “making the API work” to “designing a highly scalable, decoupled, and cost-effective serverless architecture.”
Event Experience Learning from Experienced Speakers The event allowed me to learn from professionals who have built massive systems in practice. Their perspectives helped me better understand how AWS services like Lambda and SQS are utilized in real enterprise environments, beyond basic tutorials.
Understanding Real-World Architecture Instead of just learning what a service does, the live benchmarks and architectural design patterns showed me how and why these technologies are chosen to solve scalability and cost issues in production.
Career Motivation The sessions on the internship journey and open-source contributions were highly motivating. They encouraged me to not only focus on my FCAJ project but also to start building a public portfolio of contributions, improving my ability to collaborate and work effectively in the tech industry.
Lessons Learned The most important lesson I gained from the event is that building robust cloud software requires a balance of optimal compute (Lambda) and reliable communication (SQS). A successful cloud engineer must not only master the technical implementation of these services but also cultivate a strong habit of continuous learning through real-world projects and open-source contributions. This holistic mindset will guide me as I continue to refine my legal RAG assistant and advance my career.

title: Phase 2: Backend, from Database to Lambda and API
content:
Overview Item Details Purpose A serverless backend that retrieves legal provisions, calls the LLM, and exposes a stable API. AWS services DynamoDB, Lambda, API Gateway, CloudWatch Input HTTP POST containing the user’s question Output Standard JSON with the answer or an error code Dependencies Prompt from Phase 1; Groq API key 5.4.1 Build the knowledge base on DynamoDB Goal: Store legal provisions in a table that Lambda can query.
Create the LegalArticles DynamoDB table
In the AWS Management Console, type DynamoDB in the search box and press Enter. In the left menu, select Tables, then select Create table. Table details
Table name: LegalArticles. The name must be 3 to 255 characters and may contain only letters, numbers, underscores (_), hyphens (-), and periods (.). Partition key: id, type String. This is the primary key that identifies each provision. DynamoDB hashes this value to determine where to store and find the item. Sort key (optional): leave empty, because id is the only key the table needs. Keep the default settings and select Create table. After a few seconds, the LegalArticles table becomes Active. The following steps add the provisions of Decree 13/2023/ND-CP to this table.
Prepare the IAM role for Lambda
In the AWS Management Console, type IAM in the search box and press Enter. The Security recommendations section shows that the account meets two security recommendations: MFA is enabled on the root user, and the root user has no active access keys. This follows the correct practice: enable MFA on root and work through IAM users.
The IAM resources section summarizes existing resources. The left menu includes Roles, Policies, and IAM users. We will use Roles to create a role for Lambda.
In the left menu, select Roles. This page lists the account’s roles. A role is an identity with specific permissions that uses short-term credentials and can be assumed by trusted entities such as Lambda. Select Create role on the right. Role settings
Trusted entity type: AWS service. Use case: Lambda. Permissions: attach the managed policy AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole so Lambda can write logs to CloudWatch, and add a policy that allows reading the LegalArticles table (grant only the minimum permissions needed). Role name: a recognizable name, for example legal-ai-chat-role. Select Create role. Retrieving provisions from DynamoDB (retrieve_legal_context)
5.4.2 Write the AWS Lambda function (RAG logic and Groq API) Goal: Retrieve legal context and generate the answer in a single Python function.
Create the Lambda function
In the AWS Management Console, type Lambda in the search box and press Enter. The Functions page lists the Lambda functions in the current region. Select Create function on the right. On the Create function page, select Author from scratch. Function name: legal-ai-chat-lambda. The name must be 1 to 64 characters, with no spaces, and may contain only letters, numbers, hyphens (-), and underscores (_). Runtime: Python 3.12. Permissions: by default, Lambda creates an execution role that can only write logs to CloudWatch Logs. Because this function also needs to read DynamoDB, we will use the role created in the previous step. Attach the role you created
Scroll to Additional settings and turn on Custom execution role. When enabled, the Configure custom execution role panel appears on the right. Open the Execution role list and select legal-ai-chat-role. To review the role’s permissions, select View role details in IAM. Select Save. Keep the other options, such as ARM64 architecture, Function URL, VPC, and Durable execution, turned off. We will use API Gateway instead of a Function URL. Settings marked with their own icon cannot be added or removed after the function is created. The remaining settings can be changed later.
Select Create function. The message “Successfully created the function” appears.
Write the Lambda code (lambda_function.py)
Deploy the code to Lambda
After pasting the code into lambda_function.py, select Deploy to save and apply it. The green message “Successfully updated the function legal-ai-chat-lambda” confirms the code was updated. If you do not select Deploy, Lambda keeps running the old code. Add the GROQ_API_KEY environment variable The code reads the key from the GROQ_API_KEY environment variable, so the key is not written directly in the code.
Select the Configuration tab, then select Environment variables in the left menu. The list is currently empty. Select Edit, then select Add environment variable and enter: Key: GROQ_API_KEY Value: paste the API key (gsk_…) you copied from Groq. Select Save. The system shows a success message. The GROQ_API_KEY variable is now attached to the function. If this variable is missing, the function returns error 500, “Thiếu cấu hình GROQ_API_KEY trên hệ thống” (missing GROQ_API_KEY configuration), as written in the code.
Increase the function timeout
On the Configuration tab, select General configuration, then select Edit. By default, the function has 128 MB of memory, 512 MB of ephemeral storage, and a timeout of only 3 seconds. Set Timeout to 0 min 30 sec. Three seconds is too short, because the function must query DynamoDB, call the Groq API, and wait for the model to generate the answer. If the function exceeds the timeout, Lambda stops it and the client receives an error. Keep the execution role as legal-ai-chat-role, and keep Memory at 128 MB, which is sufficient for this workshop. Scroll to the bottom and select Save. Processing flow inside the Lambda function
5.4.3 Configure API Gateway and standardize error handling Goal: Expose the Lambda function through a public HTTPS endpoint that browsers are allowed to call.
Steps
Create an API (HTTP API) with a POST route that points to the Lambda function. Configure CORS: Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to *, with the POST and OPTIONS methods. Build an error-handling layer in Lambda that returns the codes listed below. Deploy a stage and record the API call URL. Code When it occurs Meaning for the client 400 Invalid input Correct the request 429 The Groq API limit is reached Wait and retry 502 / 504 System or AI error Retry later Create an HTTP API
In the AWS Management Console, type API Gateway in the search box and press Enter. API Gateway is a fully managed service for creating, publishing, monitoring, and securing APIs at any scale. In this workshop, it serves as the public HTTPS gateway that lets the S3 website call the Lambda function.
Select Create an API in the Get started panel. On the Choose an API type page, find the HTTP API card and select Build. HTTP API offers low latency, low cost, built-in CORS support, and integration with Lambda. For this workshop, HTTP API is sufficient and cheaper than REST API.
Step 1: Configure API
API name: LegalChatAPI. IP address type: keep IPv4. Integrations: select Add integration, then choose the Lambda integration type. AWS Region: the region of the Lambda function. Lambda function: legal-ai-chat-lambda. Version: keep 2.0 (the payload format version for HTTP API). Select Next. Step 2: Configure routes A route consists of a method (HTTP verb) and a resource path.
Method: POST Resource path: /chat Integration target: legal-ai-chat-lambda Select Next. Step 3: Define stages A stage is a deployment environment for the API, such as dev or prod. The console creates the default stage $default with Auto-deploy enabled, which means every change is deployed automatically. Keep the defaults and select Next.
Step 4: Review and create Review the full configuration, then select Create.
API name: LegalChatAPI, IPv4. Integrations: legal-ai-chat-lambda (Lambda). Routes: /chat → legal-ai-chat-lambda. Stages: $default (Auto-deploy: enabled). When the API is created, the message “Successfully created API LegalChatAPI” appears.
Configure CORS CORS allows a web page on one domain (the S3 website) to call an API on another domain (API Gateway). Without this configuration, the browser blocks the request.
In the left menu, under Develop, select CORS. Initially, the fields show “No Origins/Headers/Methods are allowed,” which means nothing is permitted yet. Select Configure and enter: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: enter *, then select Add (allows every origin). Access-Control-Allow-Headers: enter content-type, then select Add. Access-Control-Allow-Methods: select POST and OPTIONS. Access-Control-Max-Age: keep 0. Allow-Credentials: keep NO. Select Save. Create the stage and deploy
Select Deploy, then create a stage named v1. The Stage details section shows the Invoke URL in the format https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com/v1. This is the base address for calling the API. Automatic Deployment for stage v1 is Disabled, so you must select Deploy manually after each configuration change. Select Deploy and choose stage v1. [Image placeholder: Deploying stage v1]
The message “Successfully created deployment for LegalChatAPI” confirms the API is live. The full URL for calling the function is:
https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com/v1/chat
5.4.4 Test the backend Goal: Confirm the backend works before connecting the interface.
Steps
Send a POST request with curl using a sample question: curl -X POST "<API_URL>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"question": "Can I use a citizen ID (CCCD) for buying and selling?"}' Open CloudWatch Logs and check the response time, the returned data, and the JSON structure. Test error cases: an empty question (400) and, if possible, a rate-limit case (429). Check: curl returns a grounded answer, and the logs show the full processing flow.

content:

title: Workshop
content:
AI Legal & Security Assistant Serverless RAG for Legal Research and Data Protection on AWS Date: 2026-11-24
Overview AI Legal & Security Assistant is a preliminary legal advisory tool for businesses. It focuses on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP on personal data protection. Users enter a question or a real-world scenario. The system searches the relevant legal provisions in a database, and then a large language model analyzes the question based only on those provisions.
The system is not a lawyer and does not provide official legal conclusions. If the database lacks a legal basis, the system must state this clearly.
The system is built on a serverless architecture with the following components:
Interface: a static web page (index.html) hosted on Amazon S3 with static website hosting. API layer: Amazon API Gateway (CORS and standardized error handling). Backend: AWS Lambda (Python), which retrieves legal provisions and calls the LLM. Knowledge base: Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles table). LLM: Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b), an external service outside AWS. Monitoring: Amazon CloudWatch. title: Security and Operations
content:
Overview Item Details Purpose Review the current security posture, monitor activity and costs, and plan improvements. AWS services CloudWatch, AWS Budgets, IAM 5.6.1 Current security posture Area Current state Risk Recommendation API Gateway Rate and burst limits set on stage v1 Anyone with the URL can call the API and exhaust the Groq quota Throttling, usage plan, or API key; add Cognito later CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * Any website can call the API from a browser Restrict to the S3 site’s origin after the demo Groq API key Stored as a Lambda environment variable Exposed if committed to code or shown in a screenshot Move to SSM Parameter Store (SecureString); rotate the key if exposed S3 website Public read, HTTP only Traffic is not encrypted Place CloudFront in front for HTTPS if needed Data sent to Groq Questions leave AWS Real customer data could leave the account Use only sample questions; review Groq’s data policy; consider Bedrock CloudWatch Lambda logging enabled Logs may contain user questions Set a 7 to 14 day retention period; avoid logging sensitive content 5.6.2 Monitoring and cost control Goal: Detect errors and unusual costs early.
Steps
Set a retention period for the Lambda log group. Create an alarm for Lambda errors (optional). Regularly review Free Tier usage in Billing and keep the Budget alert configured in section 5.2. View logs in CloudWatch
Open the CloudWatch overview page and select Logs to view the Lambda logs. In the Log groups list, select the Lambda function’s log group, which Lambda creates automatically. In the Log streams list, each stream records the function’s requests along with the time of the latest log entry. Check: test requests appear in the logs, and the Budget alert is active.
5.6.3 Security hardening roadmap Add throttling and a usage plan to the API to protect the Groq quota. This is a high priority and does not require frontend changes. Move the Groq key to SSM Parameter Store, and grant Lambda read access only to that specific parameter. Restrict CORS to the website’s origin. Add Cognito sign-in if the system moves beyond demo mode. Testing: send high-rate requests to confirm throttling, try prompt injection questions, and scan the repository for secrets. Set stage throttling limits
The stage Throttling page shows the limits in effect. Select the stage in the upper-right corner. The screenshot shows the $default stage. Each stage has its own throttling settings. Selected route throttling: limits for a specific route, overriding the default. This section is empty because no route is selected. Default route throttling: limits applied to every route in the stage. Burst and Rate limits both show “Not configured,” which means no limit is set. Account throttling: the account-wide ceiling for the region (Burst 5000, Rate 10000), shared by all APIs. This is a system-level limit and cannot be changed here. Select Edit in the Default route throttling section and set: Rate limit: 5, the maximum average number of requests per second. Burst limit: 2, the maximum number of requests processed concurrently during a sudden spike. Select Save, then select Deploy to apply the changes. [Image placeholder: Burst limit = 2 and Rate limit = 5 set on the default route]
Requests that exceed the limit receive a 429 Too Many Requests error from API Gateway, before they reach Lambda or Groq.

title: Final Results and Future Development
content: Results A complete serverless backend that scales automatically and, according to the team’s records, costs $0 under the AWS Free Tier.
